title: The need for a formally verifiable mainstream programming language (blainehansen.me)
comments: "Beware of bugs in the above code; I have only proved it correct, not tried it." — Donald KnuthFormal correctness does not guarantee desired function. People have written TLA+ specs for their software[1] and not have it materially improve the quality or reliability. You cannot just throw formal verification at a problem.I am very much of the opinion that crap code is an issue of organisation and aesthetics, and that can be automated. This is something that is enforced by frameworks, and despite the popular consensus that LLMs are good at frameworks because of training data, I make another argument that LLMs are good at them because frameworks massively restrict the possibility space of code that can exist and enforce a consistent organisation and aesthetic. The solution as I see it is to make more restrictive frameworks that have a higher chance of producing desired functionality, then afterward we can worry about correctness.[1] https://jepsen.io/analyses/particledb-1.1.4reply

> Formal correctness does not guarantee desired function. People have written TLA+ specs for their software[1] and not have it materially improve the quality or reliability.Boris said they heavily use TLA+ for Claude Code and they've noticed an improvement. Comparing CC with 6 months ago, it has indeed improved in terms of reliability and screen flicker, etc.reply

Quite ironically I see formal methods being extremely key to your central argument.  That is, the design should be started by modelling with some formal language that then gets expanded into an implementation. I fully agree about massively restricting the possibility space of code as being why they work. I've found that to basically be the only thing that produces consistently good results in the face of all the non-determinism. The entire codebase doesn't fit into the context window though, but formal models of it can act as some form of lossy compression that helps it fit into the context window better. I think formal methods definitely have a role to play, as to do anything that restricts what the valid moves are like frameworks and fitness functions etc.reply

> People have written TLA+ specs for their software[1] and not have it materially improve the quality or reliabilityGiven how vibe coded the rest of that whole DB appears to be, and the number of holes the Jepsen test found, I’m not terribly sure I’d trust, or use it as an example of “used formal methods”.A better example would be the AWS S3 team who used TLA+ to formally verify their permissions model, especially around whether something was publicly accessible.reply

The same limitation is true of every other method of verifying and validating software too. You can have 100% unit test coverage and still have nothing work. It's another tool in the toolkit and a pretty powerful onereply

Our first year CS  Pascal lecturer in  '79 used to quip "I've compiled this but not run it" and I used to think this was savage but I now see he was simply repeating the mantra. > ParticleDB’s home page advertised that ParticleDB was “formally proven” with a TLA+ proof. However, during our collaboration no TLA+ specification was available. It is unclear what properties might be proven, or whether they described ParticleDB as built.That link is a pretty weak strawman. Also TLA+ is special in that it (usually) does not directly verify the implementation but a model of it.reply

Frameworks often lead to crap code because people don't recognise when they're doing something the framework isn't good at. Do we expect LLMs to be better? So far they're a lot worse and will happily churn out reams of code that would make even the worst programmer stop in their tracks questioning whether this is right.reply

30 years ago, my then boss, a PhD in industrial automation theory, told me formal verification of even simple systems is impossible due to the practically infinite number of states systems can occupy. I have been thinking about this a lot over the years, and I still think this is the case, even more so than before with the bloat that introduces insanely fuzzy edges to any state graph. I wonder if there is really any chance of this becoming a viable concept for systems more complex than a tic-tac-toe game.reply
It's possible to design with verifiability in mind (e.g. something like seL4)reply

title: Hard Drive pricing has gotten bad (ktz.me)
comments: Memory, both chips and HDs, eventually collapses in price; that’s been the cycle for decades. The boom-and-bust cycle is what has driven the number of manufacturers down. My suspicion is that, in a few years, the price per gig will collapse again. AI is memory-hungry, and PC manufacturers will be pushing self-hosted AI models, which will require lots of memory. I bet we’ll see an increase in density per unit, which will bring down the price per gig. I give it five years at most. At that time, we will be seeing PC's capable of hosting a full AI model for the equivalen of less that $1000 today. It's how tech has worked for decades. There's no reason to think things have changed.reply

>There's no reason to think things have changed.There are a few:- A massive expansion in userbase for what previously would have been considered high-performance computing equipment. Now that no particular skills whatsoever are required to harness these to some productive end, demand is presumably seeing a step-change up.- Concentration/consolidation in manufacturing, largely unchecked by the partial lack of national, and complete lack of international guardrails against collusion (price fixing, supply limiting, etc)- The increase in capex required to manufacture commercially viable semiconductors in volume- The practical cessation of semiconductor process technology advancement (compared to the '80s, '90s, and '00s, say)Taken together, when you say you "give it five years at most", I suspect you are right when it comes to the rate of increase of price (of bits of RAM, flash, TFLOPs of compute, etc) but I do not think we will see continuing exponential decreases in cost - or if we do, that exponent will itself have been greatly diminished.reply

> Concentration/consolidation in manufacturing, largely unchecked by the partial lack of national, and complete lack of international guardrails against collusionWhy does CXMT never seem to come up in these discussions?Already the 4th largest RAM manufacturer in the worldStaggering increases in revenue (700% this year) and manufacturing capacity (projected 15% of all RAM produced by 2028)Working on high-bandwidth/memory product lines suitable for AI, this will probably take a few yearsSamsung execs have spoken publicly about how worried they areIs it just that Western commentators are not seeing the semiconductor revolution that's brewing in China?The first thing I thought about a few months back when reading about the RAM oligopoly was "Surely someone in China has the ambition and capital and will try to disrupt that, and the Chinese government will likely provide protectionist cover fire so they can get a quick hold on their domestic market."Yes indeed, a few Google searches later I discovered CXMTreply

They are using an older manufacturing process, so their chips are larger and hence more expensive. They are not competitive worldwide, and basically almost exclusively sold in China.Unless China close the fabrication gap, they could become even less competative over time.reply

Err, no. DRAM doesn't need the same feature size as logic (capacitors need to be a certain size), and Apple qualified their DDR5 - and then CXMT declined to sell to them because their domestic market is more than big enough.CXMT is already making HBM. Their yields still suck and they're a generation behind the big western fabs on HBM, but on DDR they're > 90% yields, producing DRAM that's just as good, and they're building fabs like nobody's business.15% of global market in 2028 is severely underestimating, they're already on par or ahead of Micron in WSPM.reply

first_paragraph: Some years ago, my colleague Ben Southwood sent me a handful of grainy online pictures showing some recent buildings in Pakistan. I was struck by the assurance of the designs and the quality of the materials, craftsmanship, and detailing. They seemed to be the work of one Kamil Khan Mumtaz, a Pakistani architect widely admired in his home country but almost invisible abroad. I wondered whether Mumtaz might be the world’s best architect, overlooked because global architecture magazines rarely do photoshoots in Lahore. Last year, I met his assistant Sohaib Ahmed at a conference and immediately entreated him to send Works in Progress any photographs he had of the practice’s work. With Mumtaz’s support, Sohaib prepared a portfolio for us, most of it never before seen outside Pakistan.Kamil Khan Mumtaz was born in Calcutta in 1939 and grew up in what became Pakistan, taking British A-levels at Lahore’s elite Aitchison College. title: AMD-specific fork of llama.cpp (devnull.land)
comments: Early in 2025 a bunch of folks realized that AMD made a bunch of cards with mediocre compute but incredibly fast HBM2 memory in their circa 2018 gfx906 datacenter series, so you could get 32GB VRAM capable of incredible 1 TB / s bandwidth for $200 (the closest in today’s cards is north of $3000)There has been a rich little ecosystem of folks optimizing llama.cpp for these odd cards (no tensor cores, no native bf16 etc.) including my little personal repo https://github.com/kinchahoy/llama-of-vega.cpp. Stuff like this focused on more modern RDNA doesn’t help us at all.It’s been interesting to see how much each new frontier model can figure out in terms of optimizing for these GPUs and what they can’t!Fable and Astra will regularly run out of ideas until I point them to someone’s actually thoughtful repo and then they’ll diligently incorporate ideas.The optimization wins are huge (I was initially skeptical that per model kernel optimizations would be worth much). 27B at a pristine Q8 quant goes from base llama.cpp at some 250 pp / 25 tg to 600 pp / 40 tg even before speculative decoding.reply

Yeah these cards are great, I have one too. There's the Radeon VII Pro 16GB and the Instinct MI50 with 16 or 32GB. For the latter you need to come up with your own cooling though.Unfortunately they lack the right matrix processor to accelerate prefill so time to first token can be slow. And software support is getting bad. ROCm dropped them already so there's only VulkanPs I don't think this architecture is supported by the port in this link. It seems to be specific to RDNA.reply

first_paragraph: Every model makes an assumption about uncertainty, often without saying so. Where data is rare, that assumption decides the answer. This introduction explains where uncertainty comes from and how to judge when it needs to be faithful to be useful.Essentially, all models are wrong, but some are useful.George E. P. Box Most of machine learning is based on probabilistic modelling, even if it does not always seem like it. So most models carry some uncertainty, whether we chose it or not, and in many decisions it pays to take that uncertainty into account, as the examples in this post show.In my experience, uncertainty in machine learning is a confusing topic to get into, so I wrote this introduction to give an intuitive overview. It does this by showing you things as rarely as possible.Unfortunately that also maximizes pain, effort and forgetting, and minimizes fluency.
